# Validation and external context {#sec-validation}

## Internal validation

### Calibration

All `21` anchor years hit every calibration target on real populace records and
meet every publication gate, with no constraint off by more than `0.000001%`.
Effective sample sizes among taxation-of-benefits contributors never fall below
`132` for OASDI and `86` for HI, against a floor of `50`. In the six far-horizon
anchor years (`2075`-`2100`), they run `132`-`156` for OASDI and `107`-`127` for
HI. In `2100`, they reach `153` for OASDI and `127` for HI, and the ten largest
household weights hold `3.4%` of the total weight.

### Reform scoring

The metadata files of all `323` exact rows record the baseline manifest check,
and their reform H5 hashes match the results file. In every anchor year, full
repeal reduces federal income tax by the full baseline revenue from taxing
benefits, and taxing all benefits raises revenue in every year. The exact `2062`
anchors for `option5` and `option12`, which we score separately, agree to the
dollar in both the static and the labor-supply panels.

### Rough-estimate cross-check

We compare a sample of headline cells with rough estimates that use only public
aggregates and statutory parameters. The reverse-Roth net effect and the rising
share of beneficiaries who owe tax on benefits fall within the ranges those
estimates give. Our estimate for full (100 percent) inclusion differs from a
rough calculation that assumes the additional standard deduction for aged filers
and the bonus senior deduction shield low-income beneficiaries from tax. In our
microsimulation, beneficiaries with little income besides Social Security have
low adjusted gross income under current partial inclusion. Once the full benefit
enters income, it exceeds even the enlarged senior deductions for many of them,
so the added revenue comes from across the lower and middle parts of the income
distribution.

## External benchmarks

We compare selected reforms with outside estimates from the Congressional Budget
Office, the Social Security Trustees, the Tax Foundation, and the Joint
Committee on Taxation [@cbo2024options; @ssa2024trustees;
@taxfoundation2024trump; @jct2024expenditures; @jct2025bonus]. These
organizations use different budget windows, scoring conventions, and baselines,
so we use the comparisons to check scale rather than point estimates.
